title: ACT: Science Reasoning Terms

sources.name: Original educational wording based on general subject knowledge

description: For ACT learners practicing scientific reasoning: experimental design, data interpretation, graphs, measurement, and common science terms. Original practice vocabulary, not official test questions.

cards.back: The factor deliberately changed by an experimenter to test its effect.
cards.example: A researcher changes the amount of light given to plants.

cards.back: The measured outcome that may respond to the independent variable.
cards.example: The researcher measures plant height after two weeks.

cards.back: A factor kept the same across experimental conditions.
cards.example: All plants receive the same soil and water volume.

cards.back: A comparison group that does not receive the tested treatment or receives a reference condition.
cards.example: Untreated seeds provide a comparison for fertilizer-treated seeds.

cards.back: A group exposed to the treatment or condition being tested.
cards.example: One set of seeds receives the fertilizer under investigation.

cards.back: A testable proposed explanation or prediction.
cards.example: The researcher proposes that warmer water speeds dissolving.

cards.back: A statistical claim of no effect, no difference, or no association in the population being tested.
cards.example: The initial statistical claim is that the treatment does not change mean growth.

cards.back: An expected observation derived from a hypothesis or model.
cards.example: A model predicts that doubling time at constant speed doubles distance.

cards.back: Information obtained by measurement or systematic use of the senses.
cards.example: A thermometer reads 22 degrees Celsius.

cards.back: A conclusion drawn from observations and reasoning.
cards.example: Wet soil leads a researcher to infer that rain may have fallen.

cards.back: Observations or results that help evaluate a claim.
cards.example: Repeated measurements help evaluate a claim about temperature change.

cards.back: A simplified representation of a system used to explain or predict its behavior.
cards.example: A diagram represents energy transfer through a food web.

cards.back: A broad explanation supported by extensive evidence, not merely an untested guess.
cards.example: Atomic theory explains a large body of observations about matter.

cards.back: A precise statement of how a variable is measured or manipulated.
cards.example: Germination is counted when a root first breaks through the seed coat.

cards.back: A factor that varies with the proposed cause and offers an alternative explanation for the outcome.
cards.example: Plants receiving fertilizer also receive more sunlight, obscuring the cause of faster growth.

cards.back: Assigning participants or samples to conditions by chance to reduce systematic group differences.
cards.example: A random-number generator assigns pots to treatment conditions.

cards.back: Selecting members of a population by a chance procedure to improve representativeness.
cards.example: A random draw selects addresses from a complete town list.

cards.back: Repeating a study or procedure to assess whether results are consistent.
cards.example: A second research team repeats an experiment with fresh samples.

cards.back: Multiple runs of an experimental condition, useful for estimating variability.
cards.example: The same concentration is tested in five independent runs.

cards.back: The number of independent units observed or tested.
cards.example: A study measures 40 independently selected lake samples.

cards.back: The entire group about which a study aims to draw conclusions.
cards.example: All trees in a forest are the population of interest.

cards.back: The subset of a population actually studied.
cards.example: A researcher measures 60 trees selected from that forest.

cards.back: Systematic overrepresentation or underrepresentation caused by how a sample is selected.
cards.example: Sampling only roadside trees may miss conditions deeper in the forest.

cards.back: An inactive comparison treatment designed to resemble the tested treatment.
cards.example: An inactive tablet resembles the study medicine.

cards.back: Keeping relevant people unaware of condition assignments to reduce expectation effects.
cards.example: Sample labels conceal treatment identity from the person measuring outcomes.

cards.back: A design in which both participants and the relevant researchers assessing outcomes are unaware of treatment assignment.
cards.example: Neither participants nor the relevant outcome assessors know who received the active treatment.

cards.back: A starting or reference measurement against which later measurements are compared.
cards.example: A person's resting heart rate is recorded before exercise begins.

cards.back: A condition expected to produce a known effect, showing that the procedure can detect that effect.
cards.example: A known bacterial sample checks whether a detection method works.

cards.back: A condition expected to produce no tested effect, helping reveal background responses or contamination.
cards.example: A sterile sample checks whether the procedure introduces contamination.

cards.back: Descriptive, nonnumerical observations such as color or texture.
cards.example: A solution is described as cloudy and blue.

cards.back: Numerical measurements or counts.
cards.example: A solution's temperature is recorded as 31 degrees Celsius.

cards.back: A variable with separate possible values, such as a count of seeds.
cards.example: The number of colonies on a plate takes whole-number values.

cards.back: A variable that can take values along a range, subject to measurement resolution.
cards.example: A liquid's temperature can vary continuously within a range.

cards.back: A variable whose values identify groups or labels.
cards.example: Samples are classified by soil type.

cards.back: Closeness of a measurement to the accepted or true value.
cards.example: A balance gives a value close to the certified mass of a reference weight.

cards.back: Closeness of repeated measurements to one another.
cards.example: Repeated readings cluster tightly, even if the instrument is miscalibrated.

cards.back: The smallest change a measuring device can distinguish.
cards.example: A ruler marked in millimeters cannot directly resolve micrometer differences.

cards.back: Unpredictable measurement variation that can produce scatter in either direction.
cards.example: Small unpredictable reading differences occur across repeated measurements.

cards.back: A consistent measurement distortion, such as a miscalibrated scale reading too high.
cards.example: A thermometer consistently reads two degrees too high.

cards.back: Checking or adjusting an instrument against a known reference.
cards.example: A scale is checked against a certified reference mass.

cards.back: A quantified or described range of doubt associated with a measurement or estimate.
cards.example: A reported length includes an estimated measurement interval.

cards.back: An observation unusually far from the rest; it should be investigated rather than automatically discarded.
cards.example: One reading is far above the other measurements and prompts a check of the instrument.

cards.back: The sum of values divided by their number.
cards.example: For 2, 4, and 9, the sum is 15 and the mean is 5.

cards.back: The middle value in sorted data, or the average of the two middle values when there are an even number.
cards.example: For ordered values 1, 3, and 20, the median is 3.

cards.back: The most frequently occurring value or category in a dataset.
cards.example: In 2, 2, 3, and 5, the mode is 2.

cards.back: The largest observed value minus the smallest.
cards.example: For values from 4 to 11, the range is 7.

cards.back: A measure of how spread out values are around their mean.
cards.example: Two datasets can share a mean while differing in standard deviation.

cards.back: Graphical indicators of variability or uncertainty; their meaning must be checked in the legend.
cards.example: A graph legend identifies its error bars as standard deviations.

cards.back: A general direction or pattern in data.
cards.example: The plotted temperature generally increases with time.

cards.back: An association in which higher values of one variable tend to accompany higher values of another.
cards.example: Longer plants tend to have greater mass in a sample.

cards.back: An association in which higher values of one variable tend to accompany lower values of another.
cards.example: As altitude increases, air pressure tends to decrease.

cards.back: No clear straight-line association; a nonlinear relationship may still exist.
cards.example: A U-shaped plot can lack linear correlation despite a strong patterned relationship.

cards.back: An association alone does not establish that one variable causes the other.
cards.example: Ice-cream sales and swimming both rise in warm weather without either necessarily causing the other.

cards.back: A relationship y = kx with constant ratio y/x and a graph through the origin.
cards.example: At constant speed, distance is proportional to travel time.

cards.back: A relationship y = k/x with constant product xy.
cards.example: At fixed distance, travel time is inversely proportional to speed.

cards.back: A relationship with a constant slope, expressible as y = mx + b.
cards.example: A line follows y = 3x + 2.

cards.back: A relationship whose slope is not constant across the plotted range.
cards.example: A curve follows y = x squared.

cards.back: Change in vertical value divided by change in horizontal value.
cards.example: A rise of 6 units over a run of 3 units gives a slope of 2.

cards.back: Where a graph crosses an axis; the y-intercept is the y-value when x is zero.
cards.example: For y = 3x + 2, the y-intercept is 2.

cards.back: A region in which an outcome changes little as the independent variable continues changing.
cards.example: The response curve flattens at high fertilizer concentrations.

cards.back: A value at which a response begins or changes character.
cards.example: A detector begins responding above a certain input level.

cards.back: The highest value in the stated dataset or domain.
cards.example: The largest observed temperature is the dataset's maximum.

cards.back: The lowest value in the stated dataset or domain.
cards.example: The smallest observed mass is the dataset's minimum.

cards.back: Estimating a value between observed data points.
cards.example: A value at 15 seconds is estimated from observations at 10 and 20 seconds.

cards.back: Estimating outside the observed range, often with greater uncertainty.
cards.example: A result at 100 degrees is predicted from data collected only between 20 and 40 degrees.

cards.back: Change in a quantity per unit change in another, often time.
cards.example: A tank gains 12 liters over 3 minutes, a rate of 4 liters per minute.

cards.back: The change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100 percent.
cards.example: An increase from 50 to 60 is a 20 percent increase.

cards.back: A comparison made by dividing one quantity by another.
cards.example: Six red objects to three blue objects gives a ratio of 2 to 1.

cards.back: A part divided by the whole, or an equality between two ratios, depending on context.
cards.example: If 3 of 12 samples are positive, the positive proportion is 0.25.

cards.back: A running sum of values up to a given point.
cards.example: Rainfall totals are added day by day across a month.

cards.back: The key identifying symbols, colors, or line styles.
cards.example: A key explains that dashed lines represent the control group.

cards.back: Text identifying the variable and usually its unit on a graph axis.
cards.example: An axis labeled Time (s) identifies both the quantity and its unit.

cards.back: A scale on which equal distances represent equal additive changes.
cards.example: Ticks at 0, 10, 20, and 30 are equally spaced.

cards.back: A scale on which equal distances represent equal multiplicative changes.
cards.example: Ticks at 1, 10, 100, and 1000 are equally spaced.

cards.back: An axis that begins above or below the usual reference value, potentially exaggerating visual differences.
cards.example: A vertical scale beginning at 98 can make a change from 99 to 100 look large.

cards.back: A plot of paired numerical observations used to examine relationships.
cards.example: Each point pairs a plant's height with its mass.

cards.back: A graph connecting values, often to display change across time or another ordered variable.
cards.example: A line connects temperature observations recorded in time order.

cards.back: A graph comparing values across categories using bars.
cards.example: Separate bars compare average growth in three soil categories.

cards.back: A graph showing frequencies of numerical values grouped into intervals.
cards.example: Adjacent bins show counts of organisms in size intervals.

cards.back: The number of occurrences of a value or event within a specified context.
cards.example: Seven occurrences of an event give a frequency of seven.

cards.back: The count in a category divided by the total count.
cards.example: Seven events among 20 observations give a relative frequency of 0.35.

cards.back: A label indicating the variable, condition, or unit represented by a row or column.
cards.example: A column labeled Mass (g) identifies the values below it.

cards.back: Writing a number as a coefficient times a power of ten, usually with coefficient at least 1 and less than 10 in magnitude.
cards.example: The number 4500 can be written as 4.5 times 10 to the third power.

cards.back: A scale based on powers of ten; a one-order increase is a factor of ten.
cards.example: A change from 100 to 1000 is an increase of one order of magnitude.

cards.back: Using units and conversion factors to set up or check calculations.
cards.example: Meters divided by seconds produce units of speed.

cards.back: Expressing the same quantity in a different unit by applying a conversion factor.
cards.example: Multiplying kilometers by 1000 meters per kilometer gives meters.

cards.back: Digits that communicate the precision of a reported measurement.
cards.example: Writing 2.30 grams communicates more measurement precision than writing 2.3 grams.

cards.back: Mass per unit volume.
cards.example: An object with mass 20 grams and volume 10 cubic centimeters has density 2 grams per cubic centimeter.

cards.back: The amount of a substance per specified amount of mixture or solution.
cards.example: A solution contains 5 grams of solute per liter.

cards.back: The maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a specified solvent under stated conditions.
cards.example: A stated amount dissolves in water at a specified temperature before saturation is reached.

cards.back: A condition in which a solution contains the equilibrium maximum dissolved solute under the stated conditions.
cards.example: Additional solute remains undissolved in a saturated solution at equilibrium.

cards.back: Net movement arising from random motion, typically from higher to lower concentration.
cards.example: Dye spreads through still water from a concentrated drop.

cards.back: Net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane driven by a difference in water potential.
cards.example: Water crosses a membrane toward a region of lower water potential.

cards.back: A logarithmic measure of acidity based on hydrogen ion activity; lower values are more acidic.
cards.example: A pH decrease from 4 to 3 corresponds approximately to a tenfold increase in hydrogen ion activity.

cards.back: A substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed overall.
cards.example: An enzyme increases a reaction's rate without being used up overall.

cards.back: The energy barrier that must be overcome for a reaction pathway to proceed.
cards.example: A catalyst offers a reaction pathway with a lower energy barrier.

cards.back: A dynamic state in which forward and reverse processes occur at equal rates, so macroscopic quantities remain constant.
cards.example: Reactants and products continue interconverting while their concentrations remain steady.

cards.back: A process that absorbs heat from its surroundings.
cards.example: Melting ice absorbs heat from the surroundings.

cards.back: A process that releases heat to its surroundings.
cards.example: A burning fuel releases heat to its surroundings.

cards.back: In a closed system during ordinary chemical reactions, total mass is conserved.
cards.example: A sealed reaction vessel retains the same total mass during a chemical reaction.

cards.back: Energy can be transferred or transformed but is not created or destroyed in an isolated system.
cards.example: A falling object's gravitational potential energy can become kinetic energy.

cards.back: The rate of change of position, including direction.
cards.example: A vehicle moves east at 10 meters per second.

cards.back: The rate of change of velocity.
cards.example: A vehicle's velocity increases by 2 meters per second each second.

cards.back: An interaction that can change an object's motion; net force equals mass times acceleration in Newtonian mechanics.
cards.example: For a constant mass, a greater net force produces greater acceleration.

cards.back: Force per unit area.
cards.example: The same force applied over a smaller area gives greater pressure.

cards.back: The rate of energy transfer or work done.
cards.example: Transferring 100 joules in 5 seconds corresponds to 20 watts.

cards.back: The distance between corresponding points of successive wave cycles.
cards.example: The distance from one crest to the next is one wavelength.

cards.back: The number of complete wave cycles per unit time.
cards.example: Ten cycles each second correspond to a frequency of 10 hertz.

cards.back: The maximum displacement from equilibrium for an oscillation or wave.
cards.example: A larger displacement from the equilibrium line means greater amplitude.

cards.back: The time required for half of an initial amount to decay in an exponential decay process.
cards.example: After two half-lives, one quarter of the original radioactive amount remains.

cards.back: A process in which a system's output affects its own subsequent behavior.
cards.example: A thermostat changes heating in response to the measured temperature.

cards.back: A response that opposes an initial change and can stabilize a system.
cards.example: A temperature rise causes a controller to reduce heating.

cards.back: A response that amplifies an initial change.
cards.example: An initial change triggers responses that reinforce that change.

cards.back: A resource or condition that constrains growth, rate, or another outcome.
cards.example: Low nitrogen supply can limit plant growth despite abundant light.

cards.back: The population size an environment can sustain over time under specified conditions.
cards.example: A habitat supports a population only as long as its resources and conditions permit.

cards.back: A different account that could also explain the observations.
cards.example: A temperature difference could explain a result attributed to fertilizer.

cards.back: The possibility that an observation could show a claim to be false.
cards.example: A prediction is testable when some possible observation could contradict it.

cards.back: A conclusion consistent with the evidence and limited to what the study actually tested.
cards.example: An experiment on one plant species supports a conclusion about that tested species under those conditions.

cards.back: Different proposed explanations whose predictions can be compared against evidence.
cards.example: Two accounts predict different results when light intensity changes.

cards.back: A premise taken as given in an argument or model and worth checking when interpreting its conclusions.
cards.example: A calculation assumes speed remains constant throughout the trip.
